Stated Claim / Post Context:
Ghost of Yalta returns, amid fears that Trump, Xi, and Putin will carve up Ukraine and Europe

History’s warning from Yalta hangs over today’s secretive talks, as European leaders answer an existential carve‑up threat with a clumsy committee instead of a single hard‑nosed envoy who knows the Kremlin’s playbook.

Actual Article Body:
EUobserver

Opinion

On Thursday (19 November), the US, Russian, and Chinese leaders will meet in Shenzhen, China, with no Europeans present. Europeans were also kept out of the main negotiating table at the US-mediated Russian-Ukrainian talks in Abu Dhabi last week, though their officials held separate meetings on the sidelines

Europeans will however be at the next round of Ukraine peace talks: a seeming concession by the Russians to an American request. The Europeans should beware. If the agenda is already set, they and their security will be there as an item for discussion, not as participants.

In 2021 the Kremlin demanded the de facto demilitarisation of countries that joined Nato after 1997.  Former US president Joe Biden’s administration rightly rejected that. Now US president Donald Trump’s envoys appear to be considering a much tougher set of Russian demands as part of a deal to end the Ukraine war.

The Europeans have responded to this looming threat of a new Yalta with dithering and disunity.

At the Dublin summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders of 500 million-plus people, with a combined economic weight of €28 trillion, nearly a quarter of global GDP, faced this existential question by nominating a committee: national security advisers from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland; plus officials (still unspecified) from the European Union.

It is good to have Poland on board. But a better choice would have featured, or at least explicitly included, the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. EU treaties give her, not an ad hoc committee, the foreign-policy job.

Read more

The former Estonian prime minister has an unparalleled understanding of Kremlin negotiating tactics.

And the Trump administration loathes her - another reason to insist on her presence

Diluting her role confirmed east Europeans’ feelings that “our knowledge and understanding about Russia and its erstwhile victims remain suspect when set against the fantasies and prejudices of Western Europeans,” noted Estonia’s former president Toomas Hendrik Ilves.

But in truth all Europeans are being sidelined.
